name: The A Priori
statement: Some things can be known by reason alone, independently of experience.
statementAccent: known by reason alone, independently of experience
meaning: The a priori is knowledge or justification that is independent of experience, arrived at by reason or reflection rather than on the basis of observation or the senses. A proposition is known a priori when the reason for thinking it true does not derive from experience, as with all bachelors are unmarried, that a cube has six sides, or that seven plus five equals twelve; the paradigm cases are the truths of logic and mathematics. This contrasts with a posteriori, or empirical, knowledge, which is knowable only on the basis of experience, such as that snow is white or that water boils at a certain temperature. The word a priori means prior to, or independent of, experience. An important refinement is that experience may still be needed to acquire the concepts involved in an a priori proposition, one must have the concept of a bachelor to know that bachelors are unmarried, but experience serves at most as a precondition for grasping the terms, not as the evidence that justifies the belief; the justifying reason comes from thought or reason, not from experience. The notion was central to Immanuel Kant's Critique of Pure Reason, which introduced the controversial category of the synthetic a priori, and the a priori sits at the heart of the dispute between rationalism and empiricism and of debates about the powers and limits of reason.
mechanism: The a priori marks a distinction in how a proposition is known or justified, not in its subject matter. A belief is justified a priori when the ground for holding it does not rely on experience as evidence: one can see that the proposition is true by reason, understanding, or rational insight alone, without needing to observe how the world happens to be. The classic mark of a priori truths is that they are knowable by pure thought and typically strike us as necessary and universal, holding in all cases and not merely as far as we have checked, whereas empirical generalizations are always hostage to the next observation. The crucial subtlety is the enabling role of experience. To entertain the proposition that all bachelors are unmarried one must first, through experience, acquire the concepts of bachelor and marriage; but once the concepts are in hand, no further experience is needed to justify the belief, so experience is a precondition for having the thought, not the evidence for its truth. This distinguishes the epistemological a priori from two neighboring distinctions with which it was traditionally aligned: the semantic distinction of analytic versus synthetic, concerning what makes a proposition true, and the metaphysical distinction of necessary versus contingent, concerning modal status. Kant argued that some a priori knowledge is synthetic, informative rather than merely definitional, mathematics being his prime example. Kripke later pried the distinctions apart, arguing for contingent a priori truths and necessary a posteriori truths, showing the epistemic, semantic, and metaphysical categories do not simply coincide.

examples.text: That seven plus five equals twelve, or that a cube has six sides, is known a priori, by reason rather than observation.
One needs experience to acquire the concept of a bachelor, but not to justify that bachelors are unmarried.
Kripke argued for contingent a priori and necessary a posteriori truths, prying the a priori apart from necessity.

variants.name: Analytic versus synthetic a priori
variants.text: A priori truths that hold by meaning alone, versus Kant's informative synthetic a priori, such as mathematics.

variants.name: The three distinctions
variants.text: The epistemic a priori/a posteriori, the semantic analytic/synthetic, and the metaphysical necessary/contingent, once aligned but distinct.

whyItMatters: The a priori is one of the most important notions in the theory of knowledge, because it concerns whether, and how, the mind can attain truths without the support of experience. The existence and scope of a priori knowledge is the central battleground between rationalism, which holds that reason can deliver substantive knowledge of the world independently of the senses, and empiricism, which tries to confine the a priori to the trivial or analytic and to trace all substantive knowledge to experience. Kant's Critique of Pure Reason made the a priori the pivot of modern philosophy, and his claim that there are synthetic a priori judgments, informative yet knowable without experience, such as the truths of mathematics and the principle of causation, framed epistemology for generations. The a priori also underwrites the status of logic and mathematics, which seem necessary and universal in a way observation could never establish. Twentieth-century debates, from the logical positivists' attempt to reduce the a priori to the analytic, to Quine's holist challenge to the very idea, to Kripke's separation of the a priori from the necessary and the analytic, all turn on it.

working.text: determine whether the justification for a belief derives from experience or from reason alone.
grant that experience may be needed to grasp the concepts, but not to justify the a priori belief.
distinguish the epistemic a priori from the analytic and the necessary, which need not coincide.

limits: The a priori is philosophically contested on several fronts. The deepest puzzle is how reason alone could yield knowledge of anything substantive: if a priori justification does not draw on experience, it is unclear what makes its deliverances track reality rather than merely reflect our concepts, and this is precisely why empiricists have tried to restrict the a priori to the analytic and trivial and have denied that there is any genuine synthetic a priori. W. V. O. Quine mounted the most influential modern challenge, arguing in Two Dogmas of Empiricism that the analytic-synthetic distinction on which the traditional a priori leaned cannot be non-circularly drawn and that, given confirmation holism, no statement is immune from revision in light of experience, so that the sharp category of the a priori is called into question. Even the alignment of the a priori with necessity and analyticity broke down under Kripke's arguments for the contingent a priori and the necessary a posteriori. The classical rationalism-versus-empiricism framing of these disputes is best sourced to general references rather than read verbatim from any single entry.
misreadings: The a priori is not defined by requiring no experience whatsoever; experience may be needed to acquire the relevant concepts, and what matters is only that experience is not the evidence justifying the belief. It is not the same as the analytic, since Kant argued for synthetic a priori knowledge, nor the same as the necessary, since Kripke argued for contingent a priori truths. And it is not beyond dispute, since Quine challenged the very category, so treating the a priori as needing zero experience, as identical to the analytic or the necessary, or as uncontroversial, misreads a central and debated epistemological notion.
origin: Knowledge or justification independent of experience, arrived at by reason, contrasted with the a posteriori; central to Kant's Critique of Pure Reason and to the rationalism-empiricism debate, and later reworked by Quine and Kripke.

sources.text: A Priori Justification and Knowledge, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — a priori justification as independent of experience beyond what is needed to grasp the relevant concepts, the paradigm logical and mathematical cases, Kant's synthetic a priori, and Kripke's contingent a priori and necessary a posteriori examples.

A Priori and A Posteriori, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — a priori knowledge as knowable independently of experience and a posteriori as knowable on its basis, the enabling versus justifying role of experience, the three distinct distinctions, and Quine's challenge to the a priori.
